questions.q: This lesson's security checklist has four questions. Which list matches it?
options: Authentication, authorization scope, data in transit and at rest, auditability
Code style, test coverage, deployment frequency, documentation quality
Only authentication and encryption -- the other two don't apply to integrations
Password length, two-factor adoption, browser compatibility, uptime percentage
questions.explain: The lesson's four recurring security-review questions are authentication, authorization scope, data in transit and at rest, and auditability -- a design can pass every failure-mode check from Lesson 7 and still fail on one of these.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does "least privilege" mean when applied to an integration's credential, using the Meridian ERP integration user as the example?
options: The credential should have broad access so it never needs to be reconfigured later
The integration user should be able to read exactly the fields the integration needs (catalog, price, inventory, credit hold) and nothing else the ERP exposes
Least privilege only applies to human user accounts, never to integration credentials
The ERP credential should have no access at all until manually approved on every single call
questions.explain: Least privilege applied to a system account means scoping its access to exactly what the integration actually touches -- here, catalog, price, inventory, and credit hold -- rather than a broader grant that was merely more convenient to provision.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say "the portal uses OAuth" is not a complete security answer for the Vantage Utilities case study?
options: Because OAuth answers the authentication question (who is calling) but says nothing about whether a token issued for one customer can be prevented from reading another customer's data -- that's a separate authorization-scope question
Because OAuth is not a real authentication protocol
Because Vantage Utilities does not actually use any authentication
Because authorization scope is automatically guaranteed by using OAuth
questions.explain: OAuth proves identity, which answers only the authentication question. Whether a given authenticated token can be scoped so customer A's session can't touch customer B's data is a separate authorization design-and-testing question that OAuth itself doesn't resolve.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say auditability matters most for the Harborline Capital case study specifically?
options: Because financial balance changes need to be traceable back to a source transaction ID, not just reflected as a number that changed with no record of why
Because Harborline Capital has no compliance requirements of any kind
Because auditability only matters for integrations that use Platform Events
Because Harborline's integration has no authentication requirement
questions.explain: Because the data is financial, an applied balance change needs a traceable link back to its source transaction -- an untraceable number change is exactly the kind of gap an auditor or reviewer would flag first in this case study.

questions.q: What real-world shortcut does this lesson flag as a common mistake in the Cascade Outfitters warehouse integration?
options: Using Change Data Capture instead of a scheduled delta sync
Provisioning a broad integration user "to avoid having to come back and add more objects later," which quietly defeats least privilege for convenience
Scoping the warehouse credential to exactly the objects and fields analytics needs
Running the integration during business hours instead of overnight
questions.explain: The lesson calls out over-provisioning a broad credential for convenience as a real-world shortcut that quietly violates least privilege -- exactly the kind of choice a security reviewer should catch and push back on, even though it makes future changes easier.
